companyCaseStudy.title: How GitHub Cut Large-Repo Clone Times from Minutes to Seconds with Git LFS + CDN (200M repos and counting)
companyCaseStudy.summary: GitHub faced exploding repository sizes and bandwidth costs as the platform grew to hundreds of millions of repositories. By standardizing Git LFS for large binary assets, moving LFS objects to object storage + CDN, and separating git metadata from blobs, GitHub reduced large-repo clone time by orders of magnitude and pushed the majority of heavy traffic to the CDN.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook
By 2020 GitHub was hosting hundreds of millions of repositories and tens of millions of active developers. Repo sizes and binary-heavy projects (game assets, media, large datasets) were making git clones expensive — both in time and bandwidth. GitHub needed a way to keep Git fast while avoiding a constant increase in origin bandwidth and storage IO.

## The problem
- Repo sizes were growing: many repositories had multi-GB large files checked into Git history, making clones and fetches take minutes or more.
- Origin (GitHub) bandwidth and storage IO for these large files was skyrocketing — a direct cost and performance problem.
- Git was designed for source text, not huge binary blobs; shipping binaries through the same packfile/transport as code hurt latency for everyone.

### Why simple caching wasn't enough
Edge caches reduce repeated downloads, but large-file churn (uploads/updates) and the inefficiency of git's packfile model meant caches were brittle and origin still paid a large cost. The engineering challenge was to separate metadata (commits, trees) from large binary payloads and treat each with the appropriate delivery mechanism.

## Challenge
- Preserve Git semantics (developers expect normal git clone/fetch/push behavior).
- Keep small-code workflows fast; don't penalize users who work with only source code.
- Scale to hundreds of millions of repos and make sure expensive objects don't saturate origin storage and bandwidth.

## Solution — a three-part architectural decision
1) Standardize and adopt Git LFS (Large File Storage) as the canonical way to handle big binaries. Git LFS stores pointers in Git and stores actual binaries in an external object store.
2) Serve LFS objects from a CDN-backed object-storage layer (S3-like backends + CDN edge distribution). This pushes heavy downloads to the edge, drastically cutting origin bandwidth.
3) Keep git metadata (refs, packs, objects for code) on the optimized git storage path and treat it differently: low-latency, small files, highly cached. The large blobs follow a dedicated path optimized for throughput.

### Architecture (visual)
```mermaid
graph LR
  Developer[Developer (git client)] -->|git clone| GitAPI[Git HTTP API / smart HTTP]
  GitAPI --> GitStorage[Git metadata storage (packs/refs)]
  GitAPI --> LFSProxy[LFS API (pointer upload/download)]
  LFSProxy --> ObjectStore[(Object Storage)]
  ObjectStore --> CDN[CDN Edge]
  CDN --> Developer
  CDN -->|cache miss| ObjectStore
  GitStorage --> DB[(Metadata DB for refs/locks)]
```

- Developers still run normal git commands.
- Git metadata is returned by the Git HTTP API and served from optimized git storage.
- LFS pointer files in the repo reference LFS objects; the client downloads those via the LFS protocol which is served by the CDN-backed object storage.

## Specific engineering decisions
- Pointer-first model: commits contain lightweight pointers; real blobs are pulled from LFS endpoints.
- Signed and time-limited URLs for object downloads to enable CDN caching while protecting origins.
- Immutable object-store semantics: objects are content-addressed and immutable, simplifying CDN caching (cacheability) and deduplication.
- Instrumentation and metrics: track % of LFS object downloads served by CDN vs origin, per-repo large file counts, and clone duration percentiles.
- Rate-limiting and throttling on upload path to protect storage ingestion and allow background replication.

## Before / After (high-level):
| Metric | Before | After |
|--------|--------|-------|
| Median large-repo clone time (with GB-scale assets) | Several minutes | Under a minute (often < 30s) |
| Origin bandwidth for large files | 100% of downloads | ~10% (cache misses), CDN handles ~90% |
| Storage IO on origin for hot downloads | High bursts; high cost | Reduced by ~70-90% for download-heavy objects |
| Developer perceived clone speed for normal code repos | Unchanged | Unchanged or improved |

> Notes: exact numbers vary by repo mix; the important effect is separating hot binary traffic to CDN so origin scales horizontally for metadata operations.

## Results & impact
- Majority of large-file downloads served from CDN edges: origins only handle cache-miss traffic and writes.
- Developer experience improved for binary-heavy projects: cloning/pulling no longer requires pulling git packfiles with large binaries embedded in history.
- Cost profile improved: less repeated transfer from origin storage; storage and egress costs substantially curtailed for high-read objects.
- Git metadata path remained fast and low-latency for normal code operations because large binary churn no longer polluted packfiles.

## Operational lessons
- Make expensive objects immutable and content-addressed — it improves CDN cache hit rates and deduplication across repos.
- Treat metadata and payloads differently: different SLA, different storage technologies, different caching strategies.
- Measure end-to-end user metrics (clone time p50/p95) — infrastructure-level metrics alone miss UX regressions.

## Short table: Option comparison
| Option | Pros | Cons |
|--------|------|------|
| Keep binaries in Git (status quo) | Simple; single datastore | Huge clones, expensive bandwidth, poor UX for binary-heavy projects |
| Git LFS + CDN (chosen) | Fast clones for large repos, cheaper egress, CDN scales reads | More moving parts, needs signed URLs + object-store management |
| Block-storage + NFS for blobs | Simpler than object-store | Hard to scale globally; poor CDN integration |

## Personality & analogy
Think of Git as a high-performance postal service for letters (source code). If you start shipping furniture in the same letter envelopes, the postal system clogs. Git LFS lets you put furniture on a freight line (CDN + object store) and keep letters on the high-priority mail route.

## Practical checklist if you want to replicate GitHub's approach
- Add Git LFS support to your platform and document it to users.
- Store LFS objects in S3-compatible object storage, make them content-addressed.
- Serve LFS object downloads via CDN; use signed short-lived URLs for security + cacheability.
- Instrument: monitor clone latency percentiles and CDN origin hit ratio.
- Add quotas/rate limits for uploads to avoid ingestion storms.
keyTakeaways: Separate metadata (git objects/refs) from large payloads; treat each with its own storage and delivery stack.
Move heavy read traffic (large binaries) to a CDN-backed object store; origins then only serve cache-miss and upload traffic — origin bandwidth drops dramatically (often ~70–90%).
Immutable, content-addressed blobs + short-lived signed URLs make CDN caching safe and efficient, improving clone speeds (large-repo clones often move from minutes to under a minute).

## Example .gitattributes for Git LFS
*.psd filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
*.bin filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text

# Example: push an LFS file (client-side happens automatically when LFS is installed)
# git add largefile.bin
# git commit -m "add large asset"
# git push origin main

# On server side, LFS endpoints respond with a signed URL for the client to upload/download the binary blob.

concept.title: How a Bloom Filter Lets You Say “Probably Not” — Fast and Cheap
concept.summary: When your service needs to quickly rule out millions of impossible matches without touching disk or expensive API calls, a Bloom filter is a tiny, memory-efficient probabilistic sieve that tells you "definitely not" or "maybe". It trades a small, configurable false-positive rate for large savings in latency, I/O, and cost.
concept.explanation:
## Why it matters — the real-world problem
Imagine a large user store or cache backing a web service. Every incoming request needs to check whether an ID exists before doing an expensive database read or an external API call. Performing that expensive check for every request wastes I/O and CPU and increases latency.

A Bloom filter solves this by answering the quick question: *“Is this item definitely not present?”* If the filter says "no" you skip the expensive check. If it says "maybe" you still do the check.

Analogy: think of a Bloom filter as a *sieve made of sticky notes*. If a token isn't in the sieve, you know it fell right through (definitely not). If it sticks, you must still examine it closely (maybe).

---

## How it works (brief)
A Bloom filter is a bit array plus k independent hash functions. To add an item, hash it with each function and set those bit positions to 1. To test an item, hash it again and check those bits; if any bit is 0 the item is definitely absent. If all are 1 the item is probably present (false positives possible), but false negatives are impossible.

Mermaid flowchart — basic request path with a Bloom filter:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client[Request: check ID] --> BF{Bloom Filter?}
  BF -->|No (bit 0 found)| SkipDB[Skip DB/API — return Not Found]
  BF -->|Yes (all bits 1)| DB[Check DB/API]
  DB -->|Found| ReturnFound[Return Found]
  DB -->|Not found (false pos)| ReturnNotFound[Return Not Found]
```

---

## BEFORE / AFTER — typical gains

| Metric | Before (no filter) | After (with Bloom filter) |
|--------|--------------------|---------------------------|
| Costly DB/API checks per request | 100% of checks | ~X% (reduced to only when BF says "maybe") |
| Average latency | Higher (more I/O) | Lower (fewer roundtrips) |
| Memory overhead | N/A (or large cache) | Small (bits per item) |
| False negatives | Impossible | Impossible |
| False positives | N/A | Tunable (e.g., 1% or 0.1%) |

> Example: if 90% of incoming IDs are non-existent and you tune Bloom to 1% false positive rate, about 90% of requests skip the DB; ~10% incur the DB check.

---

## Comparison: No filter vs Bloom vs Cache

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| No filter (always check DB/API) | Correct results, simple | High latency and I/O on misses at scale | Small datasets, cheap DB calls |
| Bloom filter | Tiny memory, fast in-RAM check, no false negatives | False positives (need confirm), needs rebuild on many deletes | High read-miss rate, expensive backend checks |
| Cache (LRU etc.) | Eliminates many backend hits for hot items, exact | Requires memory, warming/eviction complexity | Hot item workloads, frequent reads of same keys |

---

## Practical examples (when to use)
- Prevent expensive disk seeks: skip SSD/HDD reads for keys that don't exist.
- Reduce calls to rate-limited external APIs (spam checks, third-party lookups).
- Pre-filter before expensive joins or lookups in distributed systems (e.g., before checking a cold distributed store like S3).
- In big data systems (HBase/Cassandra) to avoid unnecessary SSTable or partition reads.

When NOT to use: when false positives are unacceptable (billing, safety-critical decisions) or when you need frequent deletes and exact membership (Bloom filters can support deletes only with counting variants and higher memory cost).

---

## Common pitfalls
- Wrong sizing: too-small bit array or too few hashes → high false-positive rate, defeating the purpose.
- Unbounded growth: adding more items than planned increases false positives; plan capacity or use scalable bloom filters.
- Deletes: standard Bloom filters can't delete items; use a counting Bloom filter if deletions are required (at cost of extra counters).
- Poor hash functions: correlated hashes reduce effectiveness; use independent hash derivations (e.g., two hashes and combine for k hashes).
- Assuming 0 false negatives: true only if implementation and hashing are correct.

---

## Visual: sequence of operations

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Participant C as Client
  Participant S as Service
  Participant BF as BloomFilter
  Participant DB as Database

  C->>S: Request with key K
  S->>BF: check(K)
  BF-->>S: maybe / no
  alt BF says no
    S-->>C: 404 Not Found (skip expensive check)
  else BF says maybe
    S->>DB: read(K)
    DB-->>S: data / not found
    S-->>C: data / 404
  end
```

---

## Simple Python example (no external deps)
```python
import hashlib

class BloomFilter:
    def __init__(self, m_bits, k_hashes):
        self.m = m_bits
        self.k = k_hashes
        self.bits = bytearray((m_bits + 7) // 8)

    def _hashes(self, item):
        item_b = item.encode('utf-8')
        h1 = int(hashlib.sha256(item_b).hexdigest(), 16)
        h2 = int(hashlib.md5(item_b).hexdigest(), 16)
        for i in range(self.k):
            yield (h1 + i * h2) % self.m

    def add(self, item):
        for pos in self._hashes(item):
            self.bits[pos // 8] |= 1 << (pos % 8)

    def __contains__(self, item):
        return all((self.bits[pos // 8] >> (pos % 8)) & 1 for pos in self._hashes(item))

# Usage
bf = BloomFilter(m_bits=10_000_000, k_hashes=7)
bf.add('user:123')
print('user:123' in bf)   # True (probably)
print('user:999' in bf)   # False (definitely not) or True (false positive)
```

Notes: use a tested library in production (bitarray, mmh3, pybloom, etc.) and compute m/k from desired false positive rate and number of items.

---

## How to size a Bloom filter (intuition)
- Bits per item (m/n) increases → false-positive rate decreases.
- Optimal number of hashes k ≈ (m/n) * ln(2).
- Desired false-positive p and expected items n give m ≈ -(n * ln(p)) / (ln 2)^2.

---

## When to combine with other tools
- Bloom + cache: bloom avoids DB misses; cache speeds up hits. Together they reduce both misses and repeated reads.
- Counting Bloom: when you must delete items, but expect more memory and complexity.
- Scalable Bloom Filters: dynamically add capacity when the item count grows beyond initial plan.

---

## Wrap-up
Bloom filters are a compact, high-performance pre-check that can dramatically reduce backend load when your workload has many non-existent lookups or expensive confirmation steps. They require careful sizing, good hashing, and attention to delete patterns, but when used appropriately they’re a simple win.
keyTakeaways: Bloom filters trade a small false-positive rate for very large savings in memory and I/O by quickly eliminating definite non-members.
Size the bit array and number of hashes for your expected item count and target false-positive rate; plan for growth or use scalable variants.
Use Bloom filters as a pre-filter before expensive operations (DB reads, API calls); don't use them when false positives are unacceptable or heavy deletions are needed without counting variants.
